rationale: B wins because it finds the human buyer story first: "the person who signs the travel policy." That is the cleanest path to a real article, not just a product-launch echo. A has muscle, but "Airbnb Moves Into Business Travel Tech, Targeting the Market Navan Built" bolts on an incumbent narrative the update did not prove. Useful, yes; a little too eager to sound like a market map.
gaps_in_A: "Targeting the Market Navan Built" overclaims the competitive frame; the update does not mention Navan, TravelPerk, Booking.com for Business, or hotel chains.
"Many Won't Qualify" is an invented headline. The facts list badge requirements, not current host qualification rates.
"the compliance gap that blocked corporate adoption" is plausible, but not supplied. That needs a travel-manager source before it can carry an angle.
The set misses the strongest buyer-led angle. "travel manager/CFO protagonist" appears inside the Concur/Ramp plumbing angle, but no angle centers the travel manager changing company policy.
gaps_in_B: "rogue Airbnb bookings on personal cards" is useful color, but it is invented color. The update does not say travel managers are fighting off-policy bookings.
"people who are often one-property operators" imports a host-market claim the update does not support.
"Airbnb goes after managed corporate lodging spend with a tool it gives away" risks overstating "free for travelers" as a free product or business-model claim.
"a legacy expense system and a newer one" is outside the supplied facts. Not fatal, but it needs confirmation before it becomes copy.
